questions.question: What is java.nio.file.Path and how do you create one?
questions.title: Path and Paths.get()
questions.direct_answer: Path is an interface in java.nio.file representing a file or directory location in the file system. You create Path instances using Path.of("config/app.properties") in Java 11+ or Paths.get("logs/output.txt") in Java 7+. Unlike the old File class, Path is immutable and works with modern NIO2 APIs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the modern NIO2 path creation API and understands Path is an interface, not a class
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using new File("path") instead of Path.of("path") in modern Java code, missing the benefits of NIO2 operations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Path is an interface with different implementations for different file systems—default file system, zip file systems, or even custom in-memory file systems

sections.title: Path: Modern Java File System Locations
sections.content:
A `Path` is simply Java's typed name for a file or folder location — like writing an address on an envelope. It lives in the **`java.nio.file`** package and arrived with Java 7's NIO2 rewrite.

**Why it exists:** the old `File` class from Java 1.0 was clunky, mutable, and tied to one file system. `Path` replaced it with a clean, **immutable** handle that pairs with the modern `Files` helper for every real operation.

**How it works:** a `Path` holds no data and touches no disk — it is pure location. You build one, then hand it to `Files` when you actually want to read or write. The two everyday constructors are:
- **`Path.of("config", "app.yml")`** — the modern way, since Java 11.
- **`Paths.get("logs/output.txt")`** — the Java 7 way, identical result.

**The nuance interviewers listen for:** `Path` is an *interface*, not a class. The default provider points at your local disk, but a zip file system or an in-memory file system can implement it too. That is why it is far more flexible than `File`.

> **The gotcha:** creating a `Path` never checks the disk. `Path.of("missing.txt")` succeeds even when the file is absent — existence checks happen only inside `Files.exists()` or a read call.

sections.title: Creating and Using Path Objects
When to Use Path
sections.content: Use Path for **all new Java file system code**—it's the standard since Java 7. Specifically: (1) **Configuration file loading**: Path makes it easy to build paths like config/dev/database.yaml without worrying about OS-specific separators. (2) **Log file management**: Create dated log paths like logs/2024-01-15/app.log using resolve() to join path segments cleanly. (3) **Resource discovery**: When your app needs to find template files, static assets, or plugins in known directory structures. Path shines when you need to manipulate locations before doing actual IO—building paths dynamically, checking relatives, or normalizing user input.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using new File() in modern code**: Freshers often write new File("config.txt") because it looks simpler, missing that Path.of("config.txt") unlocks the entire Files API with cleaner methods.
- **String concatenation for paths**: Writing basePath + "/" + fileName breaks on Windows (backslashes vs forward slashes) and looks amateur—use resolve() instead.
- **Thinking Path reads the file**: Path is just the address; calling Path.of("missing.txt") doesn't throw an exception even if the file doesn't exist. You need Files.exists(path) or Files.readString(path) to actually interact with the file system.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Interface, not class**: Path is implemented by different file system providers—default, zip, in-memory
- **Immutable**: Every path operation returns a new Path object, original stays unchanged
- **Creation**: Use Path.of("file.txt") in Java 11+ or Paths.get("file.txt") in Java 7-10
- **Platform-independent**: Path handles Windows backslashes vs Unix forward slashes automatically
- **Relative or absolute**: Path can represent both—toAbsolutePath() converts relative to absolute
- **No IO operations**: Path itself doesn't read or write files—it's just the location descriptor
- **Works with Files**: Combine with Files.readString(), Files.write(), Files.copy() for actual operations

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I'd say Path is an interface that represents a file or directory location in the file system. It's part of the NIO2 package introduced in Java 7 to replace the old File class. To create one, you use Path.of with the file path as a string—like Path.of config slash app.properties. In older Java versions before 11, you'd use Paths.get instead, but they do the same thing. The key thing about Path is that it's immutable and it doesn't actually touch the file on disk. It's just the address or location. You can create a Path for a file that doesn't even exist yet, and it won't throw an error. When you want to actually read or write the file, you use the Files utility class—like Files.readString passing in your path. One thing that trips people up is trying to use new File instead. That's the old way and you miss out on all the clean methods in the Files class. Path also handles operating system differences automatically—you don't have to worry about backslashes on Windows versus forward slashes on Linux. A cool detail is that Path is actually an interface, so different file systems can implement it differently. The default one points to your local disk, but you can have Path objects that point into zip files or even in-memory file systems. That's why it's more flexible than the old File class.

questions.question: What are the most important methods in the java.nio.file.Files utility class?
questions.title: Files Utility Class Key Methods
questions.direct_answer: The Files class is a utility with static methods for file operations. Key methods include readString and writeString for text files, readAllBytes and write for binary data, copy and move for file operations, createDirectories for folder creation, exists and isDirectory for checks, and delete for removal. It's the workhorse of modern Java file IO.

interviewer_intent.testing: Familiarity with the modern Java file operation API and whether candidate knows to use Files instead of verbose streams
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing Files exists and implementing verbose manual FileInputStream/FileOutputStream code for simple read/write operations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Files.copy with StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING to overwrite target files, and StandardCopyOption.COPY_ATTRIBUTES to preserve timestamps and permissions

sections.title: Files: Your File Operations Toolbox
sections.content:
The **`Files`** class is a toolbox of static methods that perform the actual file work — reading, writing, copying, deleting. It lives in **`java.nio.file`** and always takes a `Path` as its first argument.

**Why it exists:** before Java 7, reading one text file meant ten lines of `FileInputStream`, `BufferedReader`, and manual cleanup. `Files` turns most of that into a single call.

**How it works:** every method name says exactly what it does. The ones a fresher meets first are:
- **`Files.readString(path)`** and **`Files.writeString(path, text)`** — whole-file text, since Java 11.
- **`Files.readAllBytes(path)`** — binary data as a `byte[]`.
- **`Files.copy`**, **`Files.move`**, **`Files.createDirectories`** — file and folder operations.

**The nuance:** these methods throw a real `IOException` with a clear message. The old `File` class often just returned a silent `false`, hiding the real problem.

> **The gotcha:** `Files.readString` loads the whole file into memory. On a multi-gigabyte log it throws `OutOfMemoryError` — stream large files with `Files.lines` instead.

sections.content:
amber|Read / Write|~readString / writeString|readAllBytes / readAllLines|lines() stream|copy / move
blue|Create / Delete|~createFile / createDirectories|delete / deleteIfExists|exists / isDirectory|size
emerald|Walk / Find|~Files.walk(dir)|Files.find(...)|newDirectoryStream|walkFileTree

sections.title: Common Files Operations for Configuration and Logs
When to Use Files Methods
sections.content:
Use Files for **any standard file operation in your Java app**. Specifically: (1) **Loading configuration**: Files.readString for properties files or JSON config under 100KB—simple and readable. (2) **Writing logs**: Files.writeString with StandardOpenOption.APPEND to add log entries without complex stream handling. (3) **File system checks**: Files.exists, Files.isDirectory, Files.isReadable before attempting operations to fail fast with clear error messages. (4) **Batch operations**: Files.copy, Files.move for deployment scripts or data migration tasks where you need to reorganize files. (5) **Directory setup**: Files.createDirectories to ensure log folders or temp directories exist before writing.

Use streams directly only when processing gigabyte-sized files line by line where loading everything into memory would crash your app.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Writing manual stream code**: Freshers see FileInputStream examples online and write 15 lines of nested try-catch when Files.readString does it in one line. This wastes time and introduces resource leak bugs.
- **Forgetting Files.createDirectories**: Calling Files.writeString to logs/archive/app.log throws NoSuchFileException if the logs/archive folder doesn't exist. Always create parent directories first with createDirectories.
- **Using readString on huge files**: Files.readString loads the entire file into memory. A 2GB log file will cause OutOfMemoryError. For large files, use Files.lines which returns a stream you can process incrementally.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Utility class**: All methods are static—no need to create a Files instance
- **readString/writeString**: Java 11+ methods for text files, handle encoding automatically (UTF-8 default)
- **readAllBytes/write**: For binary data like images or PDFs, returns byte array
- **copy/move**: High-level file operations with atomic guarantees where supported by OS
- **StandardCopyOption**: REPLACE_EXISTING overwrites target, COPY_ATTRIBUTES preserves timestamps
- **createDirectories**: Makes all parent folders needed, doesn't fail if already exists
- **exists/isDirectory/isReadable**: Fast checks before operations to provide clear error messages

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The Files class is a utility in java.nio.file with static methods for all your file operations. The most important methods depend on what you're doing, but I'd highlight these. For reading and writing text files, you've got readString and writeString—these came in Java 11 and they're super clean. You pass in a Path and boom, you get the whole file as a string or write a string to a file. Before that, we had readAllLines which returns a list of strings, one per line. For binary files like images or config binaries, there's readAllBytes which gives you a byte array, and write for putting bytes back. Then for file operations, you've got copy and move. These are great because they handle all the buffering and resource management automatically. You can pass options like StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING if you want to overwrite the target file. For directory work, createDirectories is crucial—it makes all the parent folders you need in one call. It won't throw an error if the directory already exists, which is nice for setup code. There are also check methods—exists, isDirectory, isReadable. These return booleans so you can verify things before trying operations. And delete for removing files. The big mistake freshers make is not knowing Files exists at all. They write verbose FileInputStream code with try-catch-finally blocks when Files.readString does the same thing in one line. Another thing—Files handles resource cleanup automatically so you don't leak file handles. One detail that shows depth: Files.copy with COPY_ATTRIBUTES preserves the original file's timestamp and permissions, which is important for backup tools or migration scripts where you want metadata to stay intact.

questions.question: How do you traverse a directory recursively using Files.walk() in Java?
questions.title: Directory Traversal with Files.walk()
questions.direct_answer: Files.walk(path) returns a Stream of Path objects representing all files and directories under the given path in depth-first order. You must use try-with-resources to close the stream because it holds an open directory handle. Filter the stream with stream operations to find specific files, then process them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical NIO2 knowledge for directory traversal and understanding that Files.walk returns a resource that must be closed
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not closing the stream returned by Files.walk, which leaks directory handles and can cause resource exhaustion on long-running applications
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Files.walk(path, maxDepth) to limit traversal depth for performance, and Files.find() as a combined walk plus filter operation for cleaner code

sections.title: Walking Directory Trees with Files.walk
sections.content:
**`Files.walk`** lets you visit every file and folder under a directory, however deep the tree goes. It hands them back as a lazy **`Stream<Path>`**.

**Why it exists:** finding all log files or every `.java` source by hand means writing fragile recursive loops. `Files.walk` does that recursion for you, in one call.

**How it works:** starting from the root path, it descends **depth-first** — all the way down one branch before moving to the next. Because it's a stream, you shape the results with the usual operations:
- **`filter(Files::isRegularFile)`** — skip directories.
- **`filter(p -> p.toString().endsWith(".log"))`** — match an extension.
- **`forEach`** or **`toList`** — process or collect the matches.

**The nuance:** the stream holds an open directory **handle**, like an open file. That is why it must live inside a `try`-with-resources block.

> **The gotcha:** forget to close it and you leak handles. On a long-running service that ends in a *Too many open files* error after hours of work.

sections.title: Traversing with Files.walk
sections.content:
amber|Files.walk(start)|~a lazy Stream<Path>|depth-first|the whole tree by default|maxDepth optional
blue|Use|~filter(Files::isRegularFile)|map / forEach|collect matches|search by name / extension
emerald|Must|~close the stream (try-with-resources)|handle IOException|big trees need care|walkFileTree for control

sections.title: Files.walk with a depth limit and filters
Step 1: Open the Stream with Try-With-Resources
sections.content: First, call Files.walk with your starting Path inside a try-with-resources block. This guarantees the stream closes even if an exception occurs. Example: try (var paths = Files.walk(Path.of("logs"))) { ... }. The var keyword infers the type as Stream of Path. The try block ensures that when execution leaves—normally or via exception—the stream's close method runs automatically, releasing the directory handle. Without this, your stream stays open and the OS can't reclaim the resource. This matters most in long-running apps like Spring Boot services where leaked handles accumulate over days until the app can't open new files.

sections.title: Step 2: Filter and Process the Stream
sections.content: Inside the try block, use stream operations to find what you need. Common pattern: paths.filter(Files::isRegularFile) to skip directories, then filter(p -> p.toString().endsWith(".log")) to find log files, then forEach(System.out::println) to print them. You can also use map to transform paths—like map(Path::getFileName) to get just the file names. Or collect into a list: paths.filter(...).collect(Collectors.toList()). The stream is lazy, so no work happens until you call a terminal operation like forEach, collect, or count. This means you can build complex filter chains efficiently without creating intermediate collections. Once the terminal operation completes, the try block ends and the stream closes.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting try-with-resources**: Writing var paths = Files.walk(rootPath); without the try block leaks directory handles. Freshers think streams are just in-memory collections and don't realize Files.walk holds an OS resource. In production, this causes file-locked errors on Windows or "Too many open files" on Linux after hours of operation.
- **Walking entire drives**: Calling Files.walk(Path.of("/")) or Files.walk(Path.of("C:\\")) on a root directory traverses the entire file system—millions of files. The stream never completes and your app hangs. Use Files.walk(path, maxDepth) like Files.walk(logsDir, 3) to limit how deep it descends.
- **Not filtering early**: Processing every single path in a huge tree before filtering wastes time. Apply filter right after the walk call—paths.filter(Files::isRegularFile).filter(hasLogExtension)—so you only process relevant files.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Returns Stream<Path>**: Lazy stream that yields each file and directory found during traversal
- **Depth-first traversal**: Visits all descendants of a directory before moving to siblings
- **Must close**: Use try-with-resources because stream holds an open directory handle that leaks if not closed
- **Includes root**: The starting path is the first element in the stream
- **Limit depth**: Files.walk(path, maxDepth) stops at specified depth—maxDepth=1 means only immediate children
- **Follows symlinks**: By default doesn't follow symbolic links; use FileVisitOption.FOLLOW_LINKS to enable
- **Files.find alternative**: Files.find(path, maxDepth, predicate) combines walk and filter into one cleaner call

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To traverse a directory recursively, you use Files.walk passing in the starting Path. It returns a Stream of Path objects that represents all the files and directories under that location. The traversal is depth-first, meaning it goes all the way down one branch before moving to the next. The critical thing about Files.walk is you must close the stream when you're done because it holds an open directory handle to the file system. If you don't close it, you leak that handle and eventually your app can't open more files. The way to guarantee it closes is to use try-with-resources. So you'd write try open paren var paths equals Files.walk Path.of logs close paren open brace, then inside the block you process the stream with filter and forEach or whatever operations you need. For example, to find all log files, you'd do paths.filter Files colon colon isRegularFile to skip directories, then filter on the file name ending with dot-log, then forEach to process each one. Once the try block exits, the stream closes automatically. A common mistake is forgetting the try-with-resources and just calling Files.walk and storing it in a variable. That leaks resources. In a long-running Spring Boot app, after a few hours you'd start seeing errors about too many open files. Another mistake is calling Files.walk on a root directory like the C drive on Windows or slash on Linux. That tries to traverse the entire file system which can be millions of files and your app hangs. To prevent that, use Files.walk with a max depth parameter—like Files.walk logsDir comma 3 which only descends three levels deep. That's a performance saver. One extra thing to stand out: there's also Files.find which is like walk but with a built-in filter predicate. So instead of walk then filter, you pass the filter condition directly to Files.find. It's cleaner code when you know exactly what you're looking for.

questions.question: How do Path.resolve(), relativize(), and normalize() work?
questions.title: Path.resolve(), relativize(), normalize()
questions.direct_answer: resolve() appends one path to another, like basePath.resolve("logs/output.txt") to build full paths. relativize() computes the relative path from one location to another, useful for generating relative links. normalize() removes redundant dot and dot-dot segments from a path to clean it up.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Path manipulation API knowledge and whether candidate understands path algebra beyond string concatenation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to build paths with string concatenation like basePath + "/" + fileName instead of using resolve(), which breaks on different operating systems
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a concrete use case for relativize—like generating relative links in a static site generator or calculating import paths in a code analysis tool

sections.title: Path Manipulation: Resolve, Relativize, Normalize
sections.content:
**`resolve`**, **`relativize`**, and **`normalize`** are three methods on `Path` that do *path math* — they reshape locations without ever touching the disk.

The plainest version first:
- **`resolve(other)`** glues a child onto a base. `Path.of("logs").resolve("app.log")` gives `logs/app.log`.
- **`relativize(other)`** finds the route from one path to another — the inverse of resolve.
- **`normalize()`** cleans a messy path by removing `.` and `..` segments.

**Why they matter:** gluing paths with string `+` and slashes breaks across operating systems. These methods express the intent clearly and stay cross-platform.

**The nuance:** `relativize` is called on the *source* and takes the *target* — reverse them and the answer is wrong. And `normalize` works on the text only; it never follows symlinks.

> **The gotcha:** always `normalize` user-supplied paths before a security check. A value like `safe/../../etc/passwd` looks innocent until you normalize it and see it escaped the folder.

sections.title: resolve, relativize, normalize
sections.content:
amber|resolve(other)|~joins a child path|base.resolve("sub/file")|an absolute other wins|build paths safely
blue|relativize(other)|~the path FROM one TO another|inverse of resolve|produces a relative path|same base needed
emerald|normalize()|~removes . and ..|cleans redundant parts|no filesystem access|do it before comparing

sections.title: Building and Manipulating Paths
When to Use Each Method
sections.content:
Use **resolve()** when building paths dynamically—like when a config file specifies a relative log directory and you need to combine it with your app's base path. Essential for plugin systems where plugins provide relative resource paths.

Use **relativize()** when generating relative links in a static site generator—you know the absolute paths of two pages and need the href link from one to the other. Also useful in build tools when calculating import paths or in file sync tools that need to replicate directory structure but with relative references.

Use **normalize()** after accepting user input for paths or after combining paths that might contain navigation segments. If a user enters config/../secret/password.txt trying to escape the config directory, normalize reveals what they're actually requesting so you can validate it's within allowed bounds.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **String concatenation instead of resolve**: Writing baseDir + "/" + fileName fails on Windows where paths use backslashes. Freshers see the forward slash in examples and assume it works everywhere—it doesn't. Use resolve() which handles OS differences.
- **Misunderstanding relativize direction**: relativize(target) is called on the source path. Path.of("/home/user").relativize("/home/user/docs") returns docs, not the other way around. Reversing the order gives you dot-dot/dot-dot/docs which is wrong.
- **Not normalizing user input**: If your app takes a file path from the user or a config file, always normalize it before checking security boundaries. A path like allowedDir/../etc/passwd looks safe until normalized to etc/passwd which escapes your allowed directory.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **resolve(other)**: Appends other to this path—if other is absolute, returns other; if relative, joins them
- **Cross-platform**: resolve handles Windows backslashes vs Unix forward slashes automatically
- **relativize(other)**: Computes the relative path from this to other—both must be absolute or both relative
- **normalize()**: Removes redundant dot and dot-dot segments, returns cleaned path
- **Immutable**: All three return new Path instances, original paths unchanged
- **Security use case**: normalize() before security checks to detect directory traversal attempts like dot-dot-slash
- **Static site generator**: relativize() generates correct relative hrefs between HTML pages in different folders

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: These are three methods on the Path interface for manipulating file paths without hitting the file system. First, resolve appends one path onto another. You call it on a base path and pass in a relative path, and it builds the combined path. Like if you have a base directory Path.of home slash user slash app, and you call resolve on it with config slash database.yaml, you get the full path home slash user slash app slash config slash database.yaml. This is way better than string concatenation because it handles operating system differences—Windows uses backslashes, Linux uses forward slashes, resolve handles that automatically. Second method is relativize. This computes the relative path you'd need to go from one location to another. Say you have two absolute paths—source is slash home slash user slash app and target is slash home slash user slash app slash docs slash file.txt. Calling source.relativize target gives you docs slash file.txt, which is the relative path from source to target. This is super useful in static site generators where you know the absolute paths of two HTML pages and you need to generate the href link from one page to the other. It calculates the correct relative link automatically. Third is normalize. This cleans up messy paths that have redundant dot or dot-dot segments. If a path is config slash dot-dot slash logs slash dot slash output.txt, normalize removes the dot-dot which means go up one level, and the dot which means current directory, giving you just logs slash output.txt. This is important for security—if your app takes a file path from user input, you should normalize it first. Otherwise someone could enter something like allowedDir slash dot-dot slash dot-dot slash etc slash passwd trying to escape your allowed directory. After normalize you see it's actually etc slash passwd which is outside your boundaries. A common mistake with resolve is trying to use string concatenation with plus signs instead. That breaks on Windows and looks unprofessional. With relativize, people often get the direction backwards—you call it on the source and pass the target, not the other way around.

questions.question: What is WatchService in Java NIO2 and what is it used for?
questions.title: WatchService for File System Monitoring
questions.direct_answer: WatchService is a NIO2 API for monitoring directories and receiving notifications when files are created, modified, or deleted. You register a directory with the service, specifying which events to watch for, then poll or take events in a loop. It's used in hot-reload systems, configuration watchers, and development tools.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of NIO2 features beyond basic file IO, specifically file system event monitoring
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing WatchService exists and suggesting polling with Files.exists() in a loop, which is inefficient and delays detection
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Spring Boot DevTools uses WatchService internally for classpath monitoring and hot-reload, and configuration libraries like Typesafe Config use it for live reloading

sections.title: WatchService: File System Change Notifications
sections.content:
**`WatchService`** lets your program watch a folder and get told the moment a file inside it is created, changed, or deleted. It came with Java 7's NIO2.

**Why it exists:** plenty of apps must react to file changes — reloading config, picking up dropped uploads, restarting on a recompiled class. The naive fix is to poll the folder every second with `Files.exists()`, which wastes CPU and reacts late.

**How it works:** `WatchService` rides on **OS-level notifications** — `inotify` on Linux, `FSEvents` on macOS — so the kernel wakes your app only when something really changes. The loop is short:
- Register a directory for the events you care about (`ENTRY_CREATE`, `ENTRY_MODIFY`, `ENTRY_DELETE`).
- Call `take()` to block until an event arrives.
- Read the events, then call `key.reset()` to keep listening.

**The nuance:** it watches *directories*, not single files. To track one file, watch its parent and filter by name.

> **The gotcha:** forget `key.reset()` and the watcher goes silent after the first batch — it looks broken, but the key simply was not re-armed.

sections.title: WatchService at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|WatchService|~OS file-change notifications|since Java 7|register a directory|event-driven
blue|Events|~ENTRY_CREATE|ENTRY_MODIFY|ENTRY_DELETE|poll / take the WatchKey
emerald|Use|~hot-reload config|watch an upload folder|reset() the key each loop|directory-level, not recursive

sections.title: Watching a Configuration Directory
When to Use WatchService
sections.content: Use WatchService for **any scenario where your app needs to react to file changes automatically**. Specifically: (1) **Configuration hot-reload**: Watch the config directory and reload properties when the admin edits database.properties without restarting the app—critical for microservices in production. (2) **Development tools**: IDEs and build tools use WatchService to detect source file changes and trigger recompilation or hot-reload. Spring Boot DevTools internally uses it to restart your app when you change a Java class. (3) **File drop folders**: Watch an upload directory where users or external systems drop files, then process them immediately without polling. (4) **Template rendering**: Watch template directories in web frameworks—when designer edits an HTML template, re-render the page automatically. Don't use WatchService for watching thousands of directories—the registration overhead is high. For bulk monitoring, consider watching a parent directory and filtering events.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not calling key.reset()**: After processing events from a WatchKey, you must call reset() to re-enable it for future events. Forgetting this means you get one batch of events and then the watcher goes silent—your app looks broken but actually it's just the key not being reset.
- **Watching files instead of directories**: WatchService only works on directories, not individual files. If you want to watch config.properties, you register its parent directory and filter events by file name. Freshers try to register the file directly and get an exception.
- **Ignoring OVERFLOW events**: When too many changes happen rapidly, the OS can't queue them all and sends an OVERFLOW event. Your code should handle this by re-scanning the directory, not ignoring it and missing changes.
- **Running on main thread**: The watcher.take() call blocks forever waiting for events. Running this on your app's main thread freezes the UI or prevents request handling. Always run WatchService in a separate daemon thread.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **OS-level notifications**: Uses inotify (Linux), ReadDirectoryChangesW (Windows), FSEvents (macOS) for efficiency
- **Directory-only**: Registers directories, not individual files—filter events by file name to watch specific files
- **Event types**: ENTRY_CREATE (new file), ENTRY_MODIFY (content changed), ENTRY_DELETE (file removed)
- **WatchKey**: Returned when registering a directory, holds pending events for that directory
- **Must reset**: Call key.reset() after processing events or you won't receive further notifications
- **Blocking operations**: take() blocks until event occurs, poll() returns immediately with null if none
- **Spring Boot DevTools**: Uses WatchService internally for classpath monitoring and application restart triggers

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: WatchService is an API in Java NIO2 that lets you monitor a directory for file system changes and get notified when files are created, modified, or deleted. It's way more efficient than polling in a loop checking if files exist or if timestamps changed. The way it works is you create a WatchService from the default file system, then you register a directory with it specifying which events you care about—like ENTRY_CREATE, ENTRY_MODIFY, ENTRY_DELETE. After that, you run a loop calling take or poll to retrieve events. The take method blocks until something happens, while poll returns immediately with null if there's nothing. When you get an event, it tells you what kind of change occurred and which file was affected. A common use case is configuration hot-reload. Say your Spring Boot app has a config directory with properties files. You can use WatchService to watch that directory, and when the admin edits database.properties, your app gets an ENTRY_MODIFY event and reloads the configuration without restarting. This is actually how Spring Boot DevTools works internally—it watches the classpath for changes and triggers a restart when you recompile a class during development. Another use case is file drop folders. If your app has a directory where external systems or users drop files for processing, you can watch it and process files immediately instead of checking every few seconds with a scheduled task. Under the hood, WatchService uses operating system-level file system notifications—inotify on Linux, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows. These are kernel mechanisms that only notify your app when changes actually happen, so you're not wasting CPU cycles polling. A critical mistake freshers make is forgetting to call reset on the WatchKey after processing events. If you don't reset it, the key becomes invalid and you stop receiving events, and your watcher silently stops working. Another thing is WatchService only works on directories, not individual files. If you want to watch a specific file, you register its parent directory and then filter the events to only care about that file name. One detail to stand out: libraries like Typesafe Config and Apache Commons Configuration use WatchService for live config reloading, so understanding it shows you know how production tools actually work internally.

Many apps must react to file changes, like reloading config or grabbing dropped uploads. Polling every second wastes CPU and lags behind, so it's wasteful. WatchService just waits quietly instead.

Call take, which blocks until an event actually fires.
Pull the events from the key and handle each one.
Call key.reset, or the key stops sending future events.

items: Forgetting key.reset, which silently stops all further events.
Registering a single file, when WatchService only watches directories.
Running take on the main thread, which freezes the whole app.
